section: Building a Water Mask from NDWI
text:
Building a Water Mask from NDWI

A common convention is that any pixel with NDWI above 0 is more likely water than not. This is only a starting threshold, not a scientifically fixed cutoff, but it is a reasonable default for now. We build the mask the same way we filtered NumPy arrays with boolean conditions back in Session 00.


water_mask = ndwi > 0

water_pixel_count = np.sum(water_mask)
total_pixel_count = water_mask.size
water_percentage = (water_pixel_count / total_pixel_count) * 100

print(f"Water pixels: {water_pixel_count} out of {total_pixel_count} ({water_percentage:.2f}%)")

Water pixels: 421 out of 3317806 (0.01%)



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
ax.imshow(water_mask, cmap="Blues")
ax.set_title(f"Water Mask (NDWI > 0), {water_percentage:.2f}% of pixels")
plt.show()









This mask is not applied to anything yet, we are only building and inspecting it here. It gets used for real once every layer is aligned and combined into the final suitability score in Session 08, where any pixel flagged here as water is removed from consideration entirely, before scoring even happens.

Quick quiz


Question 1


Why does NDWI get used as an exclusion mask in this project, rather than as a continuous scoring factor the way NDVI is?

A. Because NDWI cannot be calculated from Sentinel-2 bands
B. Because a water pixel is not simply “less suitable”, it should not be considered a candidate site at all
C. Because NDWI values are always exactly 0 or 1
D. Because NDWI and NDVI use the same two bands, so only one can be used


Answer

B. NDVI describes a spectrum of vegetation density, where less vegetation genuinely means a somewhat better solar site, which fits a continuous score. Water is a binary, hard constraint: a pixel is either a candidate location or it is not, so it makes more sense as a mask that removes pixels entirely than as a factor that lowers their score.

NDVI and NDWI are both continuous values between -1 and 1, so the output dtype has to be float32, not the uint16 of the original Sentinel bands.


from pathlib import Path

Path("data/outputs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

output_profile = profile.copy()
output_profile.update({"dtype": "float32", "count": 1, "nodata": None})

with rasterio.open("data/outputs/ndvi.tif", "w", **output_profile) as dst:
    dst.write(ndvi, 1)

title: session 04: spectral indices, NDVI and NDWI
text:
Building indices.py

This session’s module collects everything above into reusable functions, saved into modules/indices.py. It reuses save_raster from modules/raster_utils.py, built in Session 03, rather than repeating the write logic again here.

# modules/indices.py

import rasterio
import numpy as np


def safe_divide(numerator, denominator):
    """Divide two arrays element-wise, returning 0 wherever the denominator is 0."""
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        result = np.where(denominator != 0, numerator / denominator, 0)
    return result


def calculate_ndvi(red, nir):
    """Calculate NDVI from red and near-infrared bands."""
    return safe_divide(nir - red, nir + red)


def calculate_ndwi(green, nir):
    """Calculate NDWI from green and near-infrared bands."""
    return safe_divide(green - nir, green + nir)


def load_and_calculate_indices(sentinel_path, red_band, green_band, nir_band):
    """Read the required bands from a Sentinel file and return NDVI, NDWI, and the source profile."""
    with rasterio.open(sentinel_path) as src:
        red = src.read(red_band).astype("float32")
        green = src.read(green_band).astype("float32")
        nir = src.read(nir_band).astype("float32")
        profile = src.profile

    ndvi = calculate_ndvi(red, nir)
    ndwi = calculate_ndwi(green, nir)

    return ndvi, ndwi, profile






Tip



load_and_calculate_indices is deliberately the only function here that opens a file; calculate_ndvi and calculate_ndwi work on plain NumPy arrays and know nothing about rasterio, which keeps them easy to test and reuse, for example in Session 08 when we combine multiple indices into a single suitability score.

section: A Look Ahead: xarray and rioxarray
text:
A Look Ahead: xarray and rioxarray

Everything in this session worked directly with rasterio and plain NumPy arrays: a raster’s pixel values and its geographic metadata, the CRS and transform, were always two separate things that we had to keep track of and pass around ourselves, exactly as we did with profile a moment ago. This is deliberate for a course focused on building intuition for what a raster actually is underneath. It is worth knowing, though, that a large part of the Python geospatial ecosystem has moved toward a library that fuses the two together.


xarray is a general-purpose library for working with labeled, multi-dimensional arrays, originally built for climate and atmospheric science, where a single dataset might have dimensions for latitude, longitude, time, and elevation all at once, each one labeled rather than just numbered. rioxarray extends xarray with exactly the geospatial pieces rasterio provides: CRS, transform, and raster I/O, attached directly to the array itself as metadata that travels with it automatically.


Concretely, this means a raster opened with rioxarray remembers its own CRS and transform without a separate profile dictionary being carried around by hand, and an operation such as clipping to a boundary, reprojecting, or computing NDVI can be written in a single readable expression instead of several explicit steps. For a project with only two rasters and a handful of derived layers, the way we have built things this session is easy to follow and debug. For much larger projects, especially ones involving many time steps or many bands at once, rioxarray often becomes the more practical choice, and the concepts from this course, bands, CRS, transforms, nodata, translate directly, since rioxarray is built on top of rasterio rather than replacing the ideas it represents.







Note



We do not switch to rioxarray in this course, since building the raster mental model by hand, the way we have been doing, pays off more for learning than it costs in convenience. If you want to explore it on your own afterward, the rioxarray getting started guide and the xarray documentation are both good starting points.

title: session 05: terrain analysis, slope, aspect, and hillshade
text:
Session 04 turned Sentinel bands into NDVI and NDWI, two flat, per-pixel formulas applied to spectral values. This session works with a single band, the DEM, but the math is a different kind of operation entirely: instead of comparing two bands at the same pixel, we compare each pixel to its neighbors, since slope and aspect are both properties of how elevation changes across space, not properties of a single elevation value on its own. This is the first time in the course we calculate something from a raster’s spatial structure rather than its spectral content, and that distinction is worth sitting with before writing any code.


Slope and aspect are two of the four suitability factors for the project: a gentle slope keeps installation and maintenance costs down, and a south facing slope, in the northern hemisphere, receives more direct sunlight across the day than a north facing one. Both come from the same DEM, and both come from the same underlying calculation, a gradient, so we build them together in this session.
crumbs: 6  session 05: terrain analysis, slope, aspect, and hillshade

title: session 05: terrain analysis, slope, aspect, and hillshade
text:
From Elevation to Gradient

A DEM gives us elevation, a single value per pixel. Slope and aspect both need to know how that elevation changes as we move across the grid, in the east-west direction and in the north-south direction. This rate of change is called a gradient, and it is calculated the same way a derivative is calculated in calculus: the difference in value between two nearby points, divided by the distance between them.


For a raster, “nearby points” means neighboring pixels, and “distance between them” means the pixel’s spatial resolution, the same value we pulled from transform.a and transform.e back in Session 03. This is the one detail that is easy to forget and produces a slope that looks plausible but is quantitatively wrong: the gradient has to be computed in real ground units, meters per meter, not in pixels per pixel.





Image generated with GPT Image 2.5.


import rasterio
import numpy as np

dem_path = "data/dem.tif"

with rasterio.open(dem_path) as src:
    dem = src.read(1).astype("float32")
    transform = src.transform
    profile = src.profile
    crs = src.crs
    bounds = src.bounds

print("CRS:", crs)
print("Is geographic:", crs.is_geographic)
print(transform)

CRS: EPSG:4326
Is geographic: True
| 0.00, 0.00,-2.59|
| 0.00,-0.00, 37.15|
| 0.00, 0.00, 1.00|








WarningNote: check this before trusting any slope value



Our dem.tif uses EPSG:4326, a geographic CRS, exactly the case flagged as risky back in Session 03. transform.a and transform.e here are tiny numbers, around 0.001, because they are measured in degrees, not meters, while every elevation value in the array is in meters. Feeding a meter-scale elevation difference straight into a degree-scale spacing produces a gradient many orders of magnitude too large, and arctan of a huge number saturates at 90 degrees. This is exactly why a first attempt at this calculation often produces a slope map that shows nearly every pixel at 90 degrees, a uniform, clearly wrong result, and a completely empty gentle-slope mask afterward. Always check src.crs.is_geographic before treating transform.a/transform.e as real ground distances.



The correct fix, reprojecting the DEM into a projected, meters-based CRS such as a UTM zone, is exactly the topic of Session 07, and doing it properly there means resampling the whole raster onto a new grid, not just adjusting two numbers. For this session, since we only need a reasonable pixel size in meters to get slope and aspect right, not a fully reprojected raster, we convert the degree-based resolution to an approximate meter-based one instead, using the well known fact that one degree of latitude is about 111,320 meters everywhere, while one degree of longitude shrinks as latitude increases, since meridians converge toward the poles.


if crs.is_geographic:
    center_latitude = (bounds.top + bounds.bottom) / 2
    meters_per_degree_lat = 111320
    meters_per_degree_lon = 111320 * np.cos(np.radians(center_latitude))

    x_resolution = transform.a * meters_per_degree_lon
    y_resolution = abs(transform.e) * meters_per_degree_lat
else:
    x_resolution = transform.a
    y_resolution = abs(transform.e)

print("Pixel resolution in meters (x, y):", x_resolution, y_resolution)

Pixel resolution in meters (x, y): 23.937803863467625 30.000137228455543








NoteNote: this is an approximation, not a reprojection



This conversion is only accurate near center_latitude, and gets less accurate the further a pixel is from that center latitude, or the larger the study area is. For our small study area around Desierto de Tabernas this is a perfectly reasonable stand-in, but it is not something to rely on for a large or high-latitude region, where a real reprojection to a projected CRS, as we do properly in Session 07, is the only reliable approach. Treat this cell as a practical shortcut for this session, not a technique to reuse blindly elsewhere.



np.gradient computes exactly this kind of neighbor-to-neighbor rate of change for an entire array at once, no explicit loop needed, the same vectorized spirit as every calculation so far in this course. Passed a spacing value for each axis, it divides by the correct real-world distance automatically.


dy, dx = np.gradient(dem, y_resolution, x_resolution)

print("dx shape:", dx.shape)
print("dy shape:", dy.shape)

dx shape: (605, 610)
dy shape: (605, 610)








ImportantNote: the order of np.gradient’s return values



np.gradient returns one array per axis, in the same order as the array’s own axes. For a 2D raster, axis 0 is rows, the y direction, and axis 1 is columns, the x direction, so the first array returned is dy and the second is dx. Swapping them by accident is a common source of an aspect layer that looks rotated 90 degrees from what it should be.

title: session 05: terrain analysis, slope, aspect, and hillshade
text:
Calculating Slope

Slope is the steepness of the terrain at each pixel, independent of which direction it faces. Once we have dx and dy, slope is the angle whose tangent is the combined magnitude of the two gradients, converted from radians to degrees since degrees are the more familiar unit for describing a hillside.


def calculate_slope(dx, dy):
    """Calculate slope in degrees from x and y gradients."""
    slope_radians = np.arctan(np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2))
    return np.degrees(slope_radians)


slope = calculate_slope(dx, dy)

print("Slope range:", slope.min(), "to", slope.max(), "degrees")

Slope range: 0.020481426 to 88.56868 degrees



A slope of 0 degrees means perfectly flat ground, and 90 degrees means a vertical cliff face. For a real DEM, especially one already smoothed by satellite-derived elevation processing, values will typically stay well below that, but it is worth sanity checking the maximum value against what you know about the study area, since an unexpectedly extreme slope is often a sign the resolution passed to np.gradient was wrong.
crumbs: 6  session 05: terrain analysis, slope, aspect, and hillshade

title: session 05: terrain analysis, slope, aspect, and hillshade
text:
Calculating Aspect

Aspect is the compass direction the slope faces, the direction water would flow downhill from that pixel. It comes from the same dx and dy gradients, but through arctan2, which correctly handles all four quadrants of direction rather than just a single angle.


def calculate_aspect(dx, dy):
    """Calculate aspect in degrees (0-360, 0 = north, clockwise) from x and y gradients."""
    aspect_radians = np.arctan2(dy, -dx)
    aspect_degrees = np.degrees(aspect_radians)
    aspect_degrees = (90 - aspect_degrees) % 360
    return aspect_degrees


aspect = calculate_aspect(dx, dy)

print("Aspect range:", aspect.min(), "to", aspect.max(), "degrees")

Aspect range: 0.0 to 359.99896 degrees








WarningNote: aspect convention



This course follows the standard GIS convention: 0 degrees is north, 90 is east, 180 is south, 270 is west, measured clockwise. Different libraries and textbooks sometimes define this differently, measuring counter-clockwise from east instead, so always check a formula’s convention before reusing it, and always sanity check a couple of pixels by hand against a known slope direction in your data before trusting the full output.

The Flat-Area Problem

Where a pixel is perfectly flat, both dx and dy are 0, and aspect becomes mathematically undefined, not zero, undefined, since there is no downhill direction on flat ground. arctan2(0, 0) does not raise an error, it silently returns 0, which would incorrectly show every flat pixel as facing due north. We mark these pixels explicitly instead of letting that silent default stand.


FLAT_THRESHOLD = 0.1

flat_mask = slope < FLAT_THRESHOLD
aspect[flat_mask] = -1

flat_percentage = (np.sum(flat_mask) / flat_mask.size) * 100
print(f"Flat pixels marked as -1: {flat_percentage:.2f}%")

text:
Visualizing Slope and Aspect

Slope is a sequential quantity, 0 degrees is meaningfully “less” than 40 degrees, so a sequential colormap such as "YlOrRd" fits it well: pale for gentle, dark red for steep. Aspect is different: it is a circular quantity, 359 degrees and 1 degree are almost the same direction, nearly due north, but a normal sequential colormap would show them as opposite ends of the color scale, visually implying they are as different as possible. A cyclic colormap such as "hsv" or "twilight" fixes this, wrapping smoothly back to its starting color as the value passes 360.


import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))

slope_im = axes[0].imshow(slope, cmap="YlOrRd")
axes[0].set_title("Slope (degrees)")
plt.colorbar(slope_im, ax=axes[0], label="Degrees", shrink=0.7)

aspect_display = np.ma.masked_where(aspect == -1, aspect)
aspect_im = axes[1].imshow(aspect_display, cmap="hsv", vmin=0, vmax=360)
axes[1].set_title("Aspect (degrees, flat areas masked)")
plt.colorbar(aspect_im, ax=axes[1], label="Degrees from north", shrink=0.7)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()














Tip



np.ma.masked_where builds a masked array, which imshow simply leaves transparent wherever the mask is True, rather than plotting our -1 sentinel value as if it were a real, very dark aspect. This is a cleaner way to exclude flagged pixels from a plot than filtering them out of the array entirely, since the array’s shape stays intact.

Quick quiz


Question 1


Why is a perfectly flat pixel’s aspect marked with a sentinel value like -1, rather than left at whatever arctan2(0, 0) returns?

A. Because arctan2(0, 0) raises an error and the program would crash otherwise
B. Because arctan2(0, 0) silently returns 0, which would incorrectly show every flat pixel as facing due north
C. Because flat pixels should always be excluded from the DEM entirely
D. Because aspect cannot be calculated in degrees, only in radians

section: Hillshade: Seeing the Terrain, Not Just Measuring It
text:
Hillshade: Seeing the Terrain, Not Just Measuring It

Slope and aspect are the two numbers the suitability score actually needs, but neither one, on its own, produces something that reads as a recognizable landscape at a glance. Hillshade solves a different problem: it simulates how sunlight would fall across the terrain from a chosen direction and height, producing a shaded relief image that looks like a photograph of the landscape lit from the side. It uses exactly the same slope and aspect values calculated above, combined with a light source direction, so it is a natural next step rather than a separate calculation.


matplotlib ships a ready-made tool for this, matplotlib.colors.LightSource, which takes a raw elevation array and a chosen sun azimuth, compass direction, and altitude, angle above the horizon, and returns a shaded image directly, without us needing to reimplement the illumination formula by hand.


from matplotlib.colors import LightSource

light_source = LightSource(azdeg=315, altdeg=45)

hillshade = light_source.hillshade(dem, vert_exag=1, dx=x_resolution, dy=y_resolution)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
ax.imshow(hillshade, cmap="gray")
ax.set_title("Hillshade (sun from northwest, 45 degrees altitude)")
plt.show()














TipNote: azdeg=315



An azimuth of 315 degrees, northwest, is the conventional default for hillshade in GIS software, since it tends to produce visually intuitive shading for terrain in the northern hemisphere without flattening ridgelines that happen to run in an unlucky direction. vert_exag exaggerates vertical relief, useful for a DEM with subtle elevation differences, but purely a display choice, it does not change the underlying slope or aspect values calculated earlier.



Hillshade is a display technique, not a data layer the suitability score uses directly, so it is not saved as one of the project’s terrain outputs. Its real value shows up later: in Session 09 a hillshade makes an excellent semi-transparent base layer underneath the final suitability colors, giving the interactive map real topographic texture instead of a flat colored overlay floating over a plain basemap.



Exercise 3: Light from the east


Recreate the hillshade above with the sun coming from the east instead, azdeg=90, and compare which ridgelines become more or less visible compared to the northwest version.



Solution


light_source_east = LightSource(azdeg=90, altdeg=45)
hillshade_east = light_source_east.hillshade(dem, vert_exag=1, dx=x_resolution, dy=y_resolution)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
ax.imshow(hillshade_east, cmap="gray")
ax.set_title("Hillshade (sun from east, 45 degrees altitude)")

Building terrain_analysis.py
# modules/terrain_analysis.py

import rasterio
import numpy as np


def calculate_slope(dx, dy):
    """Calculate slope in degrees from x and y gradients."""
    slope_radians = np.arctan(np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2))
    return np.degrees(slope_radians)


def calculate_aspect(dx, dy, flat_threshold=0.1, slope=None):
    """Calculate aspect in degrees (0-360, 0 = north, clockwise) from x and y gradients.
    Flat pixels (slope below flat_threshold) are marked as -1."""
    aspect_radians = np.arctan2(dy, -dx)
    aspect_degrees = np.degrees(aspect_radians)
    aspect_degrees = (90 - aspect_degrees) % 360

    if slope is not None:
        aspect_degrees[slope < flat_threshold] = -1

    return aspect_degrees


def load_and_calculate_terrain(dem_path):
    """Read a DEM and return slope, aspect, and the source profile.
    Converts pixel resolution from degrees to an approximate meters value
    if the DEM's CRS is geographic."""
    with rasterio.open(dem_path) as src:
        dem = src.read(1).astype("float32")
        transform = src.transform
        crs = src.crs
        bounds = src.bounds
        profile = src.profile

    if crs.is_geographic:
        center_latitude = (bounds.top + bounds.bottom) / 2
        meters_per_degree_lat = 111320
        meters_per_degree_lon = 111320 * np.cos(np.radians(center_latitude))
        x_resolution = transform.a * meters_per_degree_lon
        y_resolution = abs(transform.e) * meters_per_degree_lat
    else:
        x_resolution = transform.a
        y_resolution = abs(transform.e)

    dy, dx = np.gradient(dem, y_resolution, x_resolution)
    slope = calculate_slope(dx, dy)
    aspect = calculate_aspect(dx, dy, slope=slope)

    return slope, aspect, profile






Tip



Just like modules/indices.py in Session 04, the pure math functions, calculate_slope and calculate_aspect, take plain NumPy arrays and know nothing about rasterio, while load_and_calculate_terrain is the only function that touches a file directly. This split is the same pattern the whole course follows, and it is exactly what lets Session 08 import and combine functions from several modules without worrying about how each one reads its own input file.

section: Further Terrain Analysis, Beyond This Course
text:
Further Terrain Analysis, Beyond This Course

Slope, aspect, and hillshade cover what the solar suitability project actually needs, but a DEM can be pushed considerably further, and it is worth knowing what exists if you continue with terrain analysis beyond this course.


Curvature describes whether terrain is convex or concave, ridges curve one way, valleys curve the other, calculated from the second derivative of elevation rather than the first derivative slope uses. It matters for things like water flow and erosion modeling, less directly for solar siting, but it is the natural next step once slope and aspect feel comfortable, since it reuses the same gradient-based thinking one level deeper.


Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI) and Topographic Position Index (TPI) summarize how much a pixel’s elevation differs from its immediate neighbors, capturing roughness that a single slope value at one pixel does not. A moderately sloped but highly irregular patch of ground can be a worse installation site than a uniformly sloped one at the same average steepness, so a ruggedness layer is a genuinely reasonable additional suitability factor for a more advanced version of this project.


Solar radiation modeling goes a step beyond aspect alone, estimating the actual incoming solar energy a pixel would receive over a day or year, accounting for slope, aspect, latitude, time of year, and even shadows cast by surrounding terrain. This is precisely the calculation a real solar siting project would eventually want in place of the simplified aspect range rule used here. It is a substantially more involved calculation than anything in this session, typically done with a dedicated tool such as GRASS GIS’s r.sun or the Python library pysolar, rather than written from scratch.







Note



None of these three are implemented in this course, the project’s simplified slope and aspect rule is a deliberate teaching simplification, not a claim that it is the most physically accurate way to score a solar site. If you want to explore further on your own, richdem is a Python library purpose-built for exactly this kind of deeper terrain analysis, curvature, ruggedness, and flow routing included, built on the same NumPy array foundations used throughout this session.

Summary

This session turned a single elevation raster into two of the project’s four suitability factors: slope, calculated from the magnitude of the DEM’s gradient, and aspect, calculated from its direction, both derived using np.gradient in real ground units rather than raw pixel units. We handled the one genuine edge case, undefined aspect on flat ground, visualized slope with a sequential colormap and aspect with a cyclic one, and previewed the gentle-slope and south-facing masks that will feed the real suitability score in Session 08. We also built a hillshade for visual, rather than analytical, use later in Session 09, saved slope.tif and aspect.tif, built modules/terrain_analysis.py, and took a brief look at curvature, ruggedness, and solar radiation modeling as further terrain analysis beyond what this course covers. Session 06 turns to the project’s last suitability factor, distance to roads and power lines, this time built from vector data rather than a raster.

title: session 06: vector spatial analysis, buffer and access
text:
Three of our four suitability factors already exist: slope and aspect, from Session 05, and land cover, from the NDVI layer in Session 04. The fourth, access to infrastructure, is the only one that starts and mostly stays a vector problem, rather than a raster one from the beginning. road.gpkg and power.gpkg are lines, not grids, and the question we actually care about, “how close is this pixel to a road or a power line”, only becomes a raster question at the very last step of this session.


This is also the session where we go properly deeper into geopandas than Session 02 did. Reading, plotting, and checking CRS, what we did there, is the minimum needed to look at vector data. Combining and reshaping it, dissolving features by an attribute, joining two datasets by their spatial relationship rather than a shared column, and buffering, is what real vector analysis looks like, and it is the toolbox this session adds.

section: Spatial Join: Matching Features by Location, Not by Column
text:
Spatial Join: Matching Features by Location, Not by Column

An ordinary pandas join matches rows using a shared column, such as an ID. A spatial join matches rows using a geometric relationship instead, such as “this point falls inside this polygon”, with no shared column required at all. gpd.sjoin() is the tool for this, and it needs a predicate argument telling it exactly what relationship counts as a match: "within", "intersects", "contains", and a handful of others.


boundary_wgs84 = boundary.to_crs(power_points.crs)

points_with_boundary = gpd.sjoin(power_points, boundary_wgs84, predicate="within", how="left")

inside_count = points_with_boundary["index_right"].notna().sum()
outside_count = points_with_boundary["index_right"].isna().sum()

print("Power points inside boundary:", inside_count)
print("Power points outside boundary:", outside_count)

Power points inside boundary: 108
Power points outside boundary: 134








WarningNote: reproject before joining, not after



sjoin compares geometries directly, so both GeoDataFrames must already share the same CRS before the join runs, exactly like the CRS check we have run before every overlay since Session 01. We reprojected boundary to match power_points first, rather than the other way around, following the same rule from Session 01: reproject the smaller, simpler vector layer rather than an expensive raster, and here, between two vector layers, we reproject whichever one is more convenient, as long as it happens before the join.



fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
labels = ["Inside boundary", "Outside boundary"]
counts = [inside_count, outside_count]
ax.pie(counts, labels=labels, autopct="%1.1f%%", colors=["darkorange", "lightgray"])
ax.set_title("Power Points Relative to Study Area Boundary")
plt.show()









how="left" keeps every row from power_points, even the ones with no match, filling index_right with NaN for those. This is usually the safer default for a spatial join: how="inner" would silently drop every point outside the boundary, which is sometimes exactly what you want, but not something that should happen without noticing.



Exercise 2: Join with a different predicate


Repeat the spatial join above using predicate="intersects" instead of "within", and compare the resulting inside and outside counts to the ones above. For point geometries, do you expect a difference?



Solution


points_intersects = gpd.sjoin(power_points, boundary_wgs84, predicate="intersects", how="left")

inside_intersects = points_intersects["index_right"].notna().sum()
print("Inside (within):", inside_count)
print("Inside (intersects):", inside_intersects)

Inside (within): 108
Inside (intersects): 108



For point geometries against a polygon, "within" and "intersects" almost always agree, since a point has no boundary of its own to distinguish the two cases. The difference between these predicates becomes meaningful with lines and polygons, where a feature can cross a boundary without being fully inside it.

title: session 06: vector spatial analysis, buffer and access
section: Buffer: From a Feature to a Zone Around It
text:
Buffer: From a Feature to a Zone Around It

A buffer expands a geometry outward by a fixed distance in every direction, turning a line or a point into a polygon representing “everywhere within this distance of the original feature”. This is exactly the tool the access factor needs: a pixel counts as accessible if it falls inside a 1000 meter buffer around any road or power line.


roads_utm = roads.to_crs("EPSG:32629")
power_lines_utm = power_lines.to_crs("EPSG:32629")

road_buffer = roads_utm.buffer(1000)
power_buffer = power_lines_utm.buffer(1000)

print("Road buffer area (sq km):", road_buffer.area.sum() / 1_000_000)
print("Power buffer area (sq km):", power_buffer.area.sum() / 1_000_000)

Road buffer area (sq km): 4024.5305157115004
Power buffer area (sq km): 208.3558685451346








ImportantNote: buffer distance is only meaningful in a projected CRS



.buffer(1000) interprets 1000 in whatever unit the GeoDataFrame’s current CRS uses. Called on roads directly, still in EPSG:4326, this would buffer by 1000 degrees, an area covering most of the planet, not 1000 meters. This is the same mistake flagged with .length and .area back in Session 02, and it is exactly why both layers were reprojected to EPSG:32629, a meters-based UTM zone, before buffering.



Combining the Buffers

From Vector to Raster: Rasterizing the Access Zone

Every other suitability factor is already a raster, aligned to the same grid as dem.tif. The access zone, so far, is a single shapely polygon with no pixels at all. rasterio.features.rasterize() closes this gap: given a geometry and a reference grid, defined by a shape and a transform, exactly the metadata we studied in Session 03, it produces a new array marking which pixels fall inside that geometry.


import rasterio
import rasterio.features
import numpy as np

with rasterio.open("data/dem.tif") as src:
    reference_shape = (src.height, src.width)
    reference_transform = src.transform
    reference_crs = src.crs
    reference_profile = src.profile







WarningNote: the geometry must match the reference raster’s CRS



rasterize() has no awareness of CRS at all, it works purely in the reference grid’s own coordinates. access_zone is currently in EPSG:32629, from the buffering step above, while dem.tif is in EPSG:4326, as noted since Session 05. The geometry has to be reprojected to match the raster before rasterizing, or every pixel will be marked incorrectly.



from pyproj import CRS
from shapely.ops import transform as shapely_transform
from pyproj import Transformer

transformer = Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:32629", reference_crs, always_xy=True)
access_zone_dem_crs = shapely_transform(transformer.transform, access_zone)

access_raster = rasterio.features.rasterize(
    [(access_zone_dem_crs, 1)],
    out_shape=reference_shape,
    transform=reference_transform,
    fill=0,
    dtype="uint8",
)

print("Access raster shape:", access_raster.shape)
print("Accessible pixels:", np.sum(access_raster == 1))

Quick quiz


Question 2


Why does rasterize() need a reference raster’s shape and transform, rather than just the geometry itself?

A. Because rasterize() cannot work with polygons, only points
B. Because the geometry has no pixel grid of its own; the reference grid supplies the resolution and extent that turns it into pixels
C. Because the geometry must already be in raster format
D. Because rasterize() always produces a raster the same size as the geometry’s bounding box


Answer

B. A vector geometry is defined by coordinates, not pixels. rasterize() needs to be told exactly what grid, what resolution, what extent, and what alignment, to stamp that geometry onto, which is exactly the out_shape and transform supplied from the reference raster.

text:
Building spatial_analysis.py

This session’s module collects the dissolve, join, buffer, and rasterize steps above into reusable functions, saved into modules/spatial_analysis.py.

# modules/spatial_analysis.py

import geopandas as gpd
import rasterio.features
from pyproj import Transformer
from shapely.ops import transform as shapely_transform


def dissolve_by_type(gdf, column):
    """Merge features sharing the same value in a given column into one geometry per group."""
    return gdf.dissolve(by=column)


def join_within_boundary(gdf, boundary):
    """Return only the features of gdf that fall within boundary, after matching their CRS."""
    boundary_matched = boundary.to_crs(gdf.crs)
    joined = gpd.sjoin(gdf, boundary_matched, predicate="within", how="left")
    return joined[joined["index_right"].notna()]


def buffer_and_union(gdf_list, distance, projected_crs):
    """Buffer each GeoDataFrame in gdf_list by distance (in the units of projected_crs),
    then merge every resulting buffer into a single combined geometry."""
    all_buffers = []
    for gdf in gdf_list:
        gdf_projected = gdf.to_crs(projected_crs)
        all_buffers.extend(list(gdf_projected.buffer(distance)))

    combined = gpd.GeoSeries(all_buffers, crs=projected_crs)
    return combined.unary_union


def rasterize_to_reference(geometry, geometry_crs, reference_shape, reference_transform, reference_crs):
    """Rasterize a single geometry onto a reference raster's grid, reprojecting it first if needed."""
    if geometry_crs != reference_crs:
        transformer = Transformer.from_crs(geometry_crs, reference_crs, always_xy=True)
        geometry = shapely_transform(transformer.transform, geometry)

    return rasterio.features.rasterize(
        [(geometry, 1)],
        out_shape=reference_shape,
        transform=reference_transform,
        fill=0,
        dtype="uint8",
    )






Tip



Following the same split used in every module so far, dissolve_by_type and join_within_boundary work directly on GeoDataFrames with no file access, while rasterize_to_reference is the one function here that bridges vector and raster, exactly the boundary this session itself walked across.

Four suitability factors now exist on disk: ndvi.tif from Session 04, slope.tif and aspect.tif from Session 05, and access.tif from Session 06. Every one of them was built correctly for the question it was answering at the time, but none of them were built with each other in mind, and that catches up with us now. Session 08 needs to combine these four layers pixel by pixel into a single suitability score, and that operation only makes sense if pixel [120, 340] in every one of the four arrays refers to the exact same square meter of ground. This is the session several earlier notes have been pointing toward without fully resolving: the approximate degree-to-meter conversion in Session 05, the reprojection deferred at the end of Session 01, 02, and 03, and the CRS mismatches we kept fixing one pair at a time. This time we fix it properly, for all four layers at once, with a real reprojection rather than an approximation.

Watching the Mismatch Actually Break Something

It is easy to accept, in the abstract, that pixel alignment matters. It is much more convincing to watch it fail. Suppose we tried to combine two layers, still in their original form, by simple NumPy addition, exactly the kind of operation Session 08 will eventually perform for real.

Now suppose the DEM had instead been resampled to a different resolution at some point, by a teammate, a different tool, or an earlier version of this project, something that will genuinely happen over the life of a real project. To see the actual failure mode, we deliberately resample a copy of the DEM to a coarser grid and try to add it to slope.

The dangerous version of this bug is quieter: two arrays of the same shape, from two different grids, add together without any error at all, producing a suitability map that runs without complaint but scores the wrong location for every single pixel. A shape mismatch is a bug you are told about. A silent misalignment is a bug you have to go looking for, which is exactly why this session exists before Session 08, not after something goes wrong inside it.

text:
Real Reprojection with rasterio.warp

Session 05 converted the DEM’s pixel size from degrees to an approximate meters value, explicitly flagged at the time as a shortcut that only worked because we only needed a single resolution number, not a fully resampled raster. Reprojecting a raster for real means resampling every pixel onto a brand new grid, defined in a new CRS, which is a fundamentally different operation from adjusting two numbers. rasterio.warp.calculate_default_transform works out what that new grid should look like, and rasterio.warp.reproject actually resamples the data onto it.


from rasterio.warp import calculate_default_transform, reproject, Resampling

target_crs = "EPSG:32629"

with rasterio.open("data/dem.tif") as src:
    new_transform, new_width, new_height = calculate_default_transform(
        src.crs, target_crs, src.width, src.height, *src.bounds
    )
    print("New shape:", new_height, new_width)
    print("New transform:", new_transform)

New shape: 704 584
New transform: | 27.18, 0.00, 1069772.37|
| 0.00,-27.18, 4131740.26|
| 0.00, 0.00, 1.00|



calculate_default_transform does not move any pixel values yet, it only works out the shape and transform the new, projected version of this raster should have, so that its resolution in meters is comparable to the original resolution in degrees. reproject is the function that actually resamples the pixel values onto that new grid.

title: session 07: resampling, reprojection, and alignment
text:
Choosing a Resampling Method

Reprojecting always means resampling, since the new grid’s pixels almost never line up exactly with the old grid’s pixels, so a value for each new pixel has to be estimated from the pixels around it in the original. rasterio.warp.Resampling offers several strategies, and the right one depends on what kind of data is being resampled, not personal preference.







TipNote: matching the method to the data



Resampling.bilinear or Resampling.cubic blend neighboring pixel values together, which is correct for continuous data such as slope.tif, aspect.tif, or ndvi.tif, where a value halfway between two pixels really is meaningfully between them. Resampling.nearest instead copies the single closest original pixel’s value with no blending at all, which is the only correct choice for categorical data such as access.tif, a raster of 0s and 1s: blending a 0 and a 1 together would invent a meaningless value like 0.5, a pixel that is neither accessible nor inaccessible. Aspect deserves a further exception of its own, since it is circular, blending 359 degrees and 1 degree naively would average toward 180, the opposite direction, so nearest is the safer default for aspect too, despite it being continuous in principle.



resampling_choice = {
    "ndvi": Resampling.bilinear,
    "slope": Resampling.bilinear,
    "aspect": Resampling.nearest,
    "access": Resampling.nearest,
}

section: Reprojecting All Four Layers to a Shared Grid
text:
Reprojecting All Four Layers to a Shared Grid

With a target CRS and the right resampling method for each layer chosen, we reproject all four onto the exact same shape and transform, using the DEM’s own reprojected grid as the shared reference every other layer is resampled onto.


def reproject_raster(source_path, destination_path, target_crs, resampling):
    """Reproject a raster to a new CRS, writing the result to destination_path."""
    with rasterio.open(source_path) as src:
        transform, width, height = calculate_default_transform(
            src.crs, target_crs, src.width, src.height, *src.bounds
        )

        profile = src.profile.copy()
        profile.update({
            "crs": target_crs,
            "transform": transform,
            "width": width,
            "height": height,
        })

        with rasterio.open(destination_path, "w", **profile) as dst:
            reproject(
                source=rasterio.band(src, 1),
                destination=rasterio.band(dst, 1),
                src_transform=src.transform,
                src_crs=src.crs,
                dst_transform=transform,
                dst_crs=target_crs,
                resampling=resampling,
            )

    return destination_path


from pathlib import Path

Path("data/outputs/aligned").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

reprojected_paths = {}
for name, path in layers.items():
    key = name.lower()
    out_path = f"data/outputs/aligned/{key}_utm.tif"
    reproject_raster(path, out_path, target_crs, resampling_choice[key])
    reprojected_paths[name] = out_path
    print(f"Reprojected {name} -> {out_path}")

WarningNote: same CRS is still not the same grid



Reprojecting all four layers to EPSG:32629 independently, as done above, gives each one its own resolution and extent in that CRS, calculated separately by calculate_default_transform each time, which can differ slightly between layers depending on their original resolution and bounds. Sharing a CRS is necessary but not sufficient, every layer still needs to share the exact same shape and transform too, which is what the next section forces.

Resampling Everything Onto One Exact Reference Grid

We now pick one of the four reprojected layers, the DEM-derived slope layer, as the reference grid, and resample the other three directly onto its exact shape and transform, rather than each having their own independently calculated grid.


with rasterio.open(reprojected_paths["Slope"]) as ref:
    reference_shape = (ref.height, ref.width)
    reference_transform = ref.transform
    reference_crs = ref.crs
    reference_profile = ref.profile


def resample_to_reference(source_path, resampling):
    """Resample a raster directly onto the reference grid's shape, transform, and CRS."""
    with rasterio.open(source_path) as src:
        destination = np.zeros(reference_shape, dtype=src.dtypes[0])

        reproject(
            source=rasterio.band(src, 1),
            destination=destination,
            src_transform=src.transform,
            src_crs=src.crs,
            dst_transform=reference_transform,
            dst_crs=reference_crs,
            resampling=resampling,
        )

    return destination

Clipping to the Study Boundary

Every raster so far still covers a rectangular extent slightly larger than the actual study area, Desierto_de_Tabernas.gpkg. Session 01 and Session 03 only drew this boundary on top of that rectangle for a visual check. Now that every layer shares one grid, we clip all of them to that exact boundary for real, using rasterio.mask.mask, so that pixels outside the study area are excluded from the suitability score entirely, not just visually distinguished.


import geopandas as gpd
from rasterio.mask import mask

boundary = gpd.read_file("data/Desierto_de_Tabernas.gpkg")
boundary_utm = boundary.to_crs(reference_crs)


def clip_array_to_boundary(array, profile, boundary_gdf):
    """Clip an in-memory array to a boundary using an in-memory rasterio dataset."""
    with rasterio.io.MemoryFile() as memfile:
        with memfile.open(**profile) as dataset:
            dataset.write(array, 1)
            clipped, clipped_transform = mask(dataset, boundary_gdf.geometry, crop=True)

    return clipped[0], clipped_transform


clip_profile = reference_profile.copy()

clipped_arrays = {}
clipped_transform = None
for name, array in aligned_arrays.items():
    clipped_array, clipped_transform = clip_array_to_boundary(array, clip_profile, boundary_utm)
    clipped_arrays[name] = clipped_array
    print(f"{name} clipped shape:", clipped_array.shape)

mask() expects an open rasterio dataset, not a plain array, since it needs the dataset’s transform and CRS to know where the boundary geometry falls on the grid. MemoryFile lets us open a short-lived, in-memory raster dataset without ever writing an intermediate file to disk, purely to give mask() the object it expects.

text:
Confirming Everything Finally Agrees

Session 08 should never have to wonder whether its four inputs actually align. We write one function that checks shape, transform, and CRS across every layer at once, and raises a clear error the moment something does not match, rather than letting a silent mismatch slip through into a suitability score.


def check_alignment(arrays, transforms):
    """Confirm every array has the same shape and every transform is identical."""
    shapes = {name: array.shape for name, array in arrays.items()}
    unique_shapes = set(shapes.values())

    if len(unique_shapes) > 1:
        raise ValueError(f"Shape mismatch across layers: {shapes}")

    print("All layers share shape:", unique_shapes.pop())
    return True

Quick quiz


Question 1


Why is Resampling.nearest the correct choice for access.tif, but Resampling.bilinear the correct choice for ndvi.tif?

A. nearest is always faster, so it should always be preferred
B. access.tif holds categorical 0/1 values where a blended value is meaningless, while ndvi.tif holds continuous values where a blended value is a reasonable estimate
C. bilinear cannot be used on floating point rasters
D. nearest produces a smoother-looking result


Answer

B. Blending is only meaningful for continuous data. A pixel that is 70% of the way between “accessible” and “not accessible” describes nothing real, while a pixel that is 70% of the way between two NDVI values is a perfectly reasonable estimate of vegetation density at that location.




Question 2

A. Because it happens more often than a silent misalignment
B. Because Python fixes it automatically
C. Because it is loud and immediate, while two same-shaped arrays from different, misaligned grids can add together silently and produce a wrong result with no error at all
D. Because shape mismatches only happen with vector data


Answer

C. An error you are told about gets fixed before it ships. A silent misalignment between two same-shaped arrays produces a suitability map that runs perfectly and looks plausible, while scoring the wrong location for every pixel, which is far more dangerous precisely because nothing warns you.

# modules/reprojector.py

import numpy as np
import rasterio
from rasterio.warp import calculate_default_transform, reproject
from rasterio.mask import mask


def reproject_raster(source_path, destination_path, target_crs, resampling):
    """Reproject a raster to a new CRS, writing the result to destination_path."""
    with rasterio.open(source_path) as src:
        transform, width, height = calculate_default_transform(
            src.crs, target_crs, src.width, src.height, *src.bounds
        )

        profile = src.profile.copy()
        profile.update({
            "crs": target_crs,
            "transform": transform,
            "width": width,
            "height": height,
        })

        with rasterio.open(destination_path, "w", **profile) as dst:
            reproject(
                source=rasterio.band(src, 1),
                destination=rasterio.band(dst, 1),
                src_transform=src.transform,
                src_crs=src.crs,
                dst_transform=transform,
                dst_crs=target_crs,
                resampling=resampling,
            )

    return destination_path


def resample_to_reference(source_path, reference_shape, reference_transform, reference_crs, resampling):
    """Resample a raster directly onto a reference grid's shape, transform, and CRS."""
    with rasterio.open(source_path) as src:
        destination = np.zeros(reference_shape, dtype=src.dtypes[0])
        reproject(
            source=rasterio.band(src, 1),
            destination=destination,
            src_transform=src.transform,
            src_crs=src.crs,
            dst_transform=reference_transform,
            dst_crs=reference_crs,
            resampling=resampling,
        )

    return destination


def clip_array_to_boundary(array, profile, boundary_gdf):
    """Clip an in-memory array to a boundary geometry, returning the clipped array and its new transform."""
    with rasterio.io.MemoryFile() as memfile:
        with memfile.open(**profile) as dataset:
            dataset.write(array, 1)
            clipped, clipped_transform = mask(dataset, boundary_gdf.geometry, crop=True)

    return clipped[0], clipped_transform


def check_alignment(arrays):
    """Confirm every array in a dict shares the same shape. Raises ValueError otherwise."""
    shapes = {name: array.shape for name, array in arrays.items()}
    if len(set(shapes.values())) > 1:
        raise ValueError(f"Shape mismatch across layers: {shapes}")
    return True






Tip



reproject_raster and resample_to_reference look similar but solve two different steps: the first moves a raster into a new CRS with its own independently calculated grid, the second forces a raster already in the right CRS onto someone else’s exact grid. Both were needed in this session, in that order, and check_alignment is the safeguard modules/solar_suitability.py will call first, in Session 08, before doing anything else.

title: session 08: weighted overlay and the suitability model
text:
Session 07 ended with four rasters that finally share the exact same shape, transform, and CRS: slope, aspect, NDVI, and access. This session is the one the entire course has been building toward, combining those four layers into a single suitability score for every pixel, and turning that score into a map someone could actually use to decide where a solar installation makes sense.


This kind of analysis, combining several raster layers, each describing one relevant factor, into one overall score, is called a weighted overlay. It is one of the oldest and most common techniques in GIS, used for far more than solar siting: choosing a site for a new road, a hospital, a landfill, or a nature reserve all follow the same basic pattern. The specific factors change, but the underlying idea does not: decide what matters, decide how much each thing matters relative to the others, and combine them consistently across every pixel at once.

section: Why Raw Values Cannot Simply Be Added
text:
Why Raw Values Cannot Simply Be Added

It is worth pausing on why this session needs a normalization step at all, before jumping to code. Slope is measured in degrees, roughly 0 to 90. NDVI is a ratio between -1 and 1. Access is already 0 or 1. If we tried to add these three numbers directly, a single degree of slope would completely swamp the entire range of NDVI, not because slope actually matters more, but purely because its numbers happen to be bigger. Before any two measurements can be meaningfully combined, they need to be expressed on the same scale, in a way that also reflects which direction is “good” for each one.





Image generated with GPT Image 2.5.


The convention this session uses, and the standard convention in weighted overlay generally, is to rescale every factor onto the same 0 to 1 range, where 0 always means “worst for this purpose” and 1 always means “best for this purpose”, regardless of what the original units were. This step is called normalization. Once every factor speaks the same language, 0 to 1, combining them with simple arithmetic finally becomes meaningful.

text:
Normalizing Slope

Gentle slopes are good for solar installation, steep slopes are not, so slope needs an inverted normalization: low slope should map close to 1, and high slope should map close to 0. A simple, common approach is min-max normalization, rescaling the actual range of values in the data to sit between 0 and 1, then flipping it.


def normalize_slope(slope, max_slope=45):
    """Normalize slope so 0 degrees scores 1 (best) and max_slope or more scores 0 (worst)."""
    clipped = np.clip(slope, 0, max_slope)
    normalized = 1 - (clipped / max_slope)
    return normalized


slope_score = normalize_slope(layers["slope"])
print("Slope score range:", slope_score.min(), "to", slope_score.max())

Slope score range: 0.0 to 1.0








TipNote: why cap at 45 degrees, rather than the data’s own maximum



Min-max normalization is often written using the data’s own minimum and maximum, but that has a subtle problem here: if this DEM happens to contain one unusually steep outlier pixel, every other, much gentler slope would get rescaled relative to that single extreme value, compressing all the meaningful differences into a narrow band near 1. Choosing a fixed, sensible cap, 45 degrees is already far steeper than anything reasonable for solar installation, avoids letting one outlier pixel distort the scoring for every other pixel. np.clip ensures any slope beyond that cap is simply treated as equally bad, at exactly 0, rather than going negative.

title: session 08: weighted overlay and the suitability model
text:
Normalizing Aspect

Aspect needs more care than a straight min-max rescale, for the same reason flagged back in Session 05: it is a circular quantity. A south-facing slope, around 180 degrees, is ideal. As aspect moves away from 180 in either direction, east through west or west through east, suitability should fall off symmetrically, until due north, 0 or 360 degrees, is the worst possible aspect. A plain aspect / 360 would incorrectly treat 359 degrees as almost the best score, when it is actually almost due north, one of the worst.


def normalize_aspect(aspect):
    """Score aspect by closeness to south (180 degrees). Flat pixels (-1) score 0."""
    distance_from_south = np.abs(aspect - 180)
    distance_from_south = np.minimum(distance_from_south, 360 - distance_from_south)
    score = 1 - (distance_from_south / 180)

    score = np.where(aspect == -1, 0, score)
    return score


aspect_score = normalize_aspect(layers["aspect"])
print("Aspect score range:", aspect_score.min(), "to", aspect_score.max())

Aspect score range: 0.0 to 0.9999984



np.minimum(distance_from_south, 360 - distance_from_south) is the same wraparound logic used any time a circular quantity, aspect, wind direction, compass bearing, is compared to a fixed target: it takes the shorter of the two possible paths around the circle, so 359 degrees and 1 degree both correctly end up extremely close to 0 degrees, rather than at opposite ends of a straight numeric scale.







WarningNote: flat pixels do not simply score badly, they need their own rule



Recall from Session 05 that flat ground has no defined aspect at all, and was marked with the sentinel value -1, not a real compass direction. Feeding -1 into the distance formula above would produce a nonsensical result, since -1 is not a real aspect. We explicitly override every flat pixel to a fixed score, 0, after the main formula runs, rather than letting the formula guess for a case it was never designed to handle. A flat pixel that also happens to be gently sloped is still a candidate site, so a score of exactly 0 for aspect is a deliberate simplification for this course, not a claim that flat ground is truly worthless; a more advanced version of this project might score flat aspect as neutral instead of worst.

text:
Normalizing NDVI

Low NDVI, bare or scrubby ground, is preferable for this project, exactly as established back in Session 04, so NDVI also needs an inverted normalization, the same shape as slope’s, but over NDVI’s own natural range.


def normalize_ndvi(ndvi):
    """Normalize NDVI so low vegetation scores 1 (best) and high vegetation scores 0 (worst)."""
    clipped = np.clip(ndvi, -1, 1)
    normalized = 1 - ((clipped + 1) / 2)
    return normalized


ndvi_score = normalize_ndvi(layers["ndvi"])
print("NDVI score range:", ndvi_score.min(), "to", ndvi_score.max())

NDVI score range: 0.12568057 to 0.5198025



(clipped + 1) / 2 first rescales NDVI’s own -1 to 1 range onto a plain 0 to 1 range, the ordinary min-max step, since NDVI’s mathematical range is always exactly -1 to 1 regardless of the specific image, unlike slope, which has no fixed natural maximum. 1 - then flips that scale, since high NDVI, dense vegetation, should score low suitability, not high.

section: Combining the Scores: The Weighted Sum
text:
Combining the Scores: The Weighted Sum

A weight is simply a number representing how much a factor should count relative to the others, and the weights across all factors are chosen to add up to 1, so the final combined score stays within the same 0 to 1 range as each individual input. This project’s default weights, established at the start of the course, are slope 0.3, aspect 0.2, NDVI 0.3, and access 0.2, reflecting that terrain, slope and land cover, matters somewhat more for this particular project than proximity to existing infrastructure, though this is a modeling choice, not a fact about solar siting in general, which is exactly why it becomes this session’s main exercise to change.


weights = {
    "slope": 0.3,
    "aspect": 0.2,
    "ndvi": 0.3,
    "access": 0.2,
}

print("Weights sum to:", sum(weights.values()))

Weights sum to: 1.0



def calculate_final_score(slope_score, aspect_score, ndvi_score, access_score, weights):
    """Combine four normalized 0-1 layers into one weighted score, scaled to 0-100."""
    combined = (
        slope_score * weights["slope"]
        + aspect_score * weights["aspect"]
        + ndvi_score * weights["ndvi"]
        + access_score * weights["access"]
    )
    return combined * 100


suitability_score = calculate_final_score(slope_score, aspect_score, ndvi_score, access_score, weights)
print("Suitability score range:", suitability_score.min(), "to", suitability_score.max())

Suitability score range: 16.988344 to 83.36556








ImportantNote: a weighted sum is not the only way to combine factors



This project uses a weighted linear sum, the most common and easiest to explain approach: each factor contributes independently, in proportion to its weight, and a very bad score in one factor can still be outweighed by very good scores in the others. Real GIS suitability models sometimes use stricter alternatives instead, such as a weighted product, where every factor is multiplied together rather than added, so a score of 0 in any single factor forces the whole result to 0 regardless of the others. We use the additive version here because it is simpler to reason about while learning the technique, not because it is the only correct choice for every project.

Applying the Water Exclusion Mask

The NDWI water mask, built and inspected but deliberately never applied back in Session 04, finally gets used here. A pixel sitting in water is not simply penalized for it, exactly as that session explained, it should be removed from consideration entirely, regardless of how favorably every other factor scored it. We rebuild the mask here, since it was not one of the four factor layers carried through Session 07’s alignment, and apply it directly to the final score.


with rasterio.open("data/sentinel.tif") as src:
    green = src.read(2).astype("float32")
    nir = src.read(4).astype("float32")

with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    ndwi = np.where((green + nir) != 0, (green - nir) / (green + nir), 0)

water_mask = ndwi > 0

Water pixels in original grid: 421

Applying it directly to suitability_score would silently reintroduce the exact misalignment problem Session 07 exists to prevent. In a full project, this mask would be run through the same resample_to_reference step from modules/reprojector.py before use. For this session, since building the full mask is a repeat of Session 04’s own steps, we take the shortcut of resampling only the boolean mask itself with nearest-neighbor resampling, the correct method for categorical data, exactly as decided in Session 07.

        source=water_mask_uint8,
        destination=aligned_water_mask,
        src_transform=src.transform,
        src_crs=src.crs,
        dst_transform=reference_profile["transform"],
        dst_crs=reference_profile["crs"],

text:
Classifying the Final Map

A continuous 0 to 100 score is precise, but a decision maker usually wants a simpler answer: is this location suitable or not. We split the continuous score into three classes using fixed thresholds, following the project’s original plan: below 40 is unsuitable, 40 to 70 is moderate, and above 70 is suitable.


def classify_suitability(score, low_threshold=40, high_threshold=70):
    """Classify a continuous suitability score into 3 classes: 0=unsuitable, 1=moderate, 2=suitable."""
    classified = np.zeros_like(score, dtype="uint8")
    classified[(score >= low_threshold) & (score < high_threshold)] = 1
    classified[score >= high_threshold] = 2
    return classified


suitability_class = classify_suitability(suitability_score)
class_labels = {0: "Unsuitable", 1: "Moderate", 2: "Suitable"}







TipNote: np.zeros_like



np.zeros_like(score, dtype="uint8") creates a new array with the same shape as score, but filled with 0 and stored as an 8-bit unsigned integer, appropriate for a layer that only ever needs to hold the values 0, 1, or 2. This is the same pattern as np.zeros() from Session 00, except the shape is copied from an existing array rather than typed out by hand, which matters here since we do not want to risk a typo producing a shape that quietly does not match suitability_score.

Why must every factor be normalized to the same 0-1 range before applying weights, rather than combining the raw slope, aspect, NDVI, and access values directly?

A. Because numpy cannot add arrays with different data types
B. Because each factor’s raw values use different units and ranges, so a weight applied to unnormalized numbers would not actually reflect the intended importance of each factor
C. Because normalization is required for rasterio to save a file
D. Because only integer arrays can be combined with weights


Answer

B. A weight is only meaningful relative to a shared scale. Applying a weight of 0.3 to slope, measured in tens of degrees, and 0.3 to NDVI, measured between -1 and 1, would not give them equal influence at all, since their raw numbers are wildly different sizes to begin with.




Question 2


Why is the water mask applied after the weighted sum, by forcing masked pixels to 0, rather than built into calculate_final_score as a fifth weighted factor?

A. Because NDWI cannot be normalized to a 0-1 range
B. Because a weighted factor only ever nudges a score up or down, while water needs to remove a pixel from consideration entirely, exactly the distinction made back in Session 04
C. Because numpy does not support more than four arrays in a weighted sum
D. Because water pixels always have the lowest NDVI value


Answer

B. This is the same reasoning introduced in Session 04’s quiz: NDVI describes a spectrum where a partial penalty makes sense, but a water pixel is a hard exclusion, not a matter of degree. A weight, no matter how large, can always be outweighed by the other factors; an explicit mask cannot.

text:
Building solar_suitability.py
# modules/solar_suitability.py

import numpy as np


def normalize_slope(slope, max_slope=45):
    """Normalize slope so 0 degrees scores 1 (best) and max_slope or more scores 0 (worst)."""
    clipped = np.clip(slope, 0, max_slope)
    return 1 - (clipped / max_slope)


def normalize_aspect(aspect):
    """Score aspect by closeness to south (180 degrees). Flat pixels (-1) score 0."""
    distance_from_south = np.abs(aspect - 180)
    distance_from_south = np.minimum(distance_from_south, 360 - distance_from_south)
    score = 1 - (distance_from_south / 180)
    return np.where(aspect == -1, 0, score)


def normalize_ndvi(ndvi):
    """Normalize NDVI so low vegetation scores 1 (best) and high vegetation scores 0 (worst)."""
    clipped = np.clip(ndvi, -1, 1)
    return 1 - ((clipped + 1) / 2)


def calculate_final_score(slope_score, aspect_score, ndvi_score, access_score, weights):
    """Combine four normalized 0-1 layers into one weighted score, scaled to 0-100."""
    combined = (
        slope_score * weights["slope"]
        + aspect_score * weights["aspect"]
        + ndvi_score * weights["ndvi"]
        + access_score * weights["access"]
    )
    return combined * 100


def apply_water_mask(score, water_mask):
    """Force any pixel flagged as water to a score of 0, regardless of its other factors."""
    return np.where(water_mask == 1, 0, score)


def classify_suitability(score, low_threshold=40, high_threshold=70):
    """Classify a continuous suitability score into 3 classes: 0=unsuitable, 1=moderate, 2=suitable."""
    classified = np.zeros_like(score, dtype="uint8")
    classified[(score >= low_threshold) & (score < high_threshold)] = 1
    classified[score >= high_threshold] = 2
    return classified






Tip



Every function here works on plain NumPy arrays, following the same split as every module before it: the parts of this session that actually open files, in the notebook above, stay separate from the parts that only do math, which is what makes it possible for Session 09 to import classify_suitability and reuse it without needing to know anything about how suitability.tif was produced.

This session combined everything the project has built so far into one result. We normalized slope, aspect, and NDVI onto a shared 0-1 scale, each with a rule specific to what “good” means for that factor, left access unchanged since it was already on that scale, and combined all four with a weighted sum into a single 0-100 suitability score. title: datasets
text:
Every other dataset in this project is downloaded relative to a single boundary polygon. This boundary can come from a file you already have (a .gpkg you drew yourself, for example in geojson.io), or it can be generated automatically by geocoding a place name through OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim service, which OSMnx wraps in a single function call. Using a boundary file gives you precise control over the exact shape and size of the study area. Geocoding a place name is faster to get started with, but returns the official administrative boundary of that place, which can be far larger than what you actually want for a class exercise, so it is worth checking the size before committing to it.

from pathlib import Path
import geopandas as gpd
import osmnx as ox
from shapely.ops import unary_union

DATA_DIR = Path("data")
DATA_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

BOUNDARY_GPKG_PATH = None
PLACE_NAME = "Tabernas, Almería, Spain"

if BOUNDARY_GPKG_PATH is not None and Path(BOUNDARY_GPKG_PATH).exists():
    boundary_gdf = gpd.read_file(BOUNDARY_GPKG_PATH)
else:
    boundary_gdf = ox.geocode_to_gdf(PLACE_NAME)

if boundary_gdf.crs is None:
    boundary_gdf = boundary_gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
elif boundary_gdf.crs.to_epsg() != 4326:
    boundary_gdf = boundary_gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

if len(boundary_gdf) > 1:
    study_polygon = unary_union(boundary_gdf.geometry)
else:
    study_polygon = boundary_gdf.geometry.iloc[0]

print("Boundary bounds:", study_polygon.bounds)

boundary_gdf.to_file(DATA_DIR / "boundary.gpkg", driver="GPKG")






TipWhy EPSG:4326



The boundary is kept in EPSG:4326 (plain latitude and longitude) because this is the coordinate system that Earth Engine expects when a region is passed to it. Reprojecting into a metric CRS happens later, in Session 3 and Session 7, once we actually need to measure distances or areas in meters.

text:
Digital Elevation Model, Copernicus GLO-30

The DEM provides elevation values across the study area and is the source for two of the four suitability factors used later in the project: slope and aspect. This course uses Copernicus GLO-30, a global elevation model at 30 meter resolution, produced from radar data collected during the TanDEM-X mission between 2010 and 2015. It is one of the most widely used free global DEMs available today, alongside alternatives such as SRTM and ALOS World 3D, and is accessible directly through Google Earth Engine under the collection id COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30_2024_1.







WarningAbout the dataset version



The original Earth Engine collection COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30 has been deprecated and replaced by COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30_2024_1. The year in the new name refers to when this edition of the dataset was reprocessed and republished, not to when the elevation was measured. The underlying radar data is still from 2010 to 2015. For natural terrain that has not been reshaped by mining, landslides, or large construction, this age difference has no meaningful effect on slope or aspect calculations. More detail is available on the Copernicus DEM overview page.



Technically, GLO30 is a Digital Surface Model rather than a Digital Terrain Model, meaning that in areas with buildings or dense vegetation, the elevation includes the height of what sits on top of the ground, not only the bare earth. Since this project specifically targets barren or low vegetation land for solar panel placement, this distinction rarely causes a practical problem.

import ee
import geemap

ee.Authenticate()
ee.Initialize(project="YOUR-GEE-PROJECT-ID")

aoi = geemap.geopandas_to_ee(boundary_gdf).geometry()

dem_collection = ee.ImageCollection("COPERNICUS/DEM/GLO30_2024_1")
dem = dem_collection.select("DEM").mosaic().clip(aoi)

dem_output_path = DATA_DIR / "dem.tif"

geemap.ee_export_image(
    dem,
    filename=str(dem_output_path),
    scale=30,
    region=aoi,
    crs="EPSG:4326",
    file_per_band=False,
)






TipDirect download versus Google Drive export



geemap.ee_export_image downloads the raster straight to local disk and works well for small study areas, but Earth Engine limits how large a single direct download can be, roughly a few hundred megabytes. For a study area covering an entire province rather than a few square kilometers, this limit is exceeded and the export must instead go through ee.batch.Export.image.toDrive, which has no practical size limit but requires retrieving the finished file from Google Drive afterward, and often splits large exports into several tiles that need to be merged back together with rasterio.merge.

text:
Sentinel-2 Surface Reflectance Imagery

Sentinel-2 provides the multispectral imagery used to calculate NDVI, which distinguishes vegetated land from barren or sparsely vegetated land, one of the four suitability factors in this project. This course uses the Sentinel-2 Level-2A collection, which is already corrected for atmospheric effects (surface reflectance rather than top-of-atmosphere reflectance), avoiding the need to apply that correction manually. On Earth Engine this is the COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED collection.


A single Sentinel-2 scene is rarely usable on its own because of cloud cover, so the acquisition script filters the full image collection down to scenes with less than a chosen cloud cover percentage over a date range, masks out any remaining cloud and cloud shadow pixels using the Scene Classification Layer (SCL) band, and then takes the pixel-wise median across all remaining scenes. The result is a single, mostly cloud-free composite image rather than one individual acquisition, which is far more reliable for a fixed teaching dataset than trying to find one perfect scene by hand.

def mask_s2_clouds(image):
    scl = image.select("SCL")
    mask = scl.neq(3).And(scl.neq(8)).And(scl.neq(9)).And(scl.neq(10))
    return image.updateMask(mask)

DATE_START = "2024-01-01"
DATE_END = "2024-12-31"
MAX_CLOUD_PERCENT = 10

s2_collection = (
    ee.ImageCollection("COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED")
    .filterBounds(aoi)
    .filterDate(DATE_START, DATE_END)
    .filter(ee.Filter.lt("CLOUDY_PIXEL_PERCENTAGE", MAX_CLOUD_PERCENT))
    .map(mask_s2_clouds)
)

print("Number of matching scenes:", s2_collection.size().getInfo())

s2_image = s2_collection.median().clip(aoi)
s2_export = s2_image.select(["B2", "B3", "B4", "B8"])

sentinel_output_path = DATA_DIR / "sentinel.tif"

geemap.ee_export_image(
    s2_export,
    filename=str(sentinel_output_path),
    scale=10,
    region=aoi,
    crs="EPSG:4326",
    file_per_band=False,
)

Only four of the twelve available Sentinel-2 bands are exported: B2 (blue), B3 (green), B4 (red), and B8 (near infrared). Red and near infrared are the two bands NDVI actually needs, while blue and green are kept along for true color visualization purposes in later sessions. A full band description is available on the official Sentinel-2 bands reference.







WarningWhat the SCL mask numbers mean



The Scene Classification Layer assigns every pixel a class code. This project excludes class 3 (cloud shadow), class 8 (cloud, medium probability), class 9 (cloud, high probability), and class 10 (thin cirrus). Pixels in any of these classes are set to no data rather than included in the composite, since they do not represent the true reflectance of the ground.

title: datasets
text:
Road Network, OpenStreetMap

Roads represent one half of the infrastructure accessibility factor: land close to existing roads is more practical and less costly to develop for solar installations, since it is easier to reach for construction and maintenance. This course retrieves roads through OSMnx, a Python library that queries OpenStreetMap data through the Overpass API and returns it directly as a GeoDataFrame, without needing to manually download and clip an extract of an entire country.

import osmnx as ox

road_graph = ox.graph_from_polygon(study_polygon, network_type="drive")
_, roads = ox.graph_to_gdfs(road_graph)

roads_clipped = gpd.clip(roads, boundary_gdf)
roads_clipped.to_file(DATA_DIR / "roads.gpkg", driver="GPKG")

print("Roads saved:", len(roads_clipped), "segments")

The network_type="drive" argument restricts the result to roads that vehicles can travel on, excluding footpaths, cycleways, and similar minor ways that are irrelevant to construction access. OpenStreetMap coverage quality varies significantly by region: countries with an active mapping community, much of Western Europe among them, tend to have dense and reliable road data, while more remote areas may have gaps. It is worth visually inspecting the downloaded roads before relying on them for analysis.







TipOverpass server availability



OSMnx queries a public Overpass API server by default, which occasionally becomes temporarily unreachable under heavy load. If a connection error appears, switching to a mirror server, for example by setting ox.settings.overpass_endpoint = "https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter" before making the request, usually resolves it. More endpoints are listed on the Overpass API wiki page.

title: datasets
text:
Power Line Network, OpenStreetMap

Power lines represent the second half of the infrastructure accessibility factor: proximity to existing electrical infrastructure directly affects how expensive it is to connect a new solar installation to the grid. This data also comes from OpenStreetMap, using OSMnx’s more general feature query function rather than the road-specific graph function, since power infrastructure is not a routable network but a collection of tagged features.

power_tags = {"power": ["line", "minor_line"]}
power_lines = ox.features_from_polygon(study_polygon, tags=power_tags)

power_lines = power_lines[power_lines.geom_type.isin(["LineString", "MultiLineString"])]

power_clipped = gpd.clip(power_lines, boundary_gdf)
power_clipped.to_file(DATA_DIR / "power_lines.gpkg", driver="GPKG")

print("Power lines saved:", len(power_clipped), "segments")

OpenStreetMap tags high voltage transmission lines as power=line and lower voltage local distribution lines as power=minor_line. Both are retrieved here since either type of line represents a usable grid connection point for this project. The query also returns some point features, such as individual poles or towers tagged with the same power key, which are filtered out afterward since only the line geometries themselves are relevant to a distance-based suitability factor. Full tagging conventions for power infrastructure are documented on the OpenStreetMap power wiki page.

title: datasets
text:
Going Beyond This Course’s Datasets

The datasets described on this page were deliberately kept simple: a single free elevation model, one cloud-filtered Sentinel-2 composite, and two OpenStreetMap layers. This choice is intentional. The course is meant to be approachable regardless of your background, so every dataset here can be downloaded in minutes, without specialized access requests, licensing negotiations, or heavy preprocessing. None of it requires prior remote sensing expertise to obtain or interpret.


That said, this is far from the only reasonable way to build a solar site suitability model. The academic and industry literature on renewable energy site selection uses a considerably richer set of inputs, and if you want to push this project further, it is worth exploring some of them. A few directions to look into:


Solar irradiance data, such as the Global Solar Atlas or Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service products, which measure actual sunlight availability rather than assuming it is uniform across the study area.
Higher resolution or radar-derived DEMs, such as national LiDAR-based elevation datasets where available, which can resolve terrain features far more precisely than a 30 meter global model.
Land cover and land use datasets, such as ESA WorldCover or Corine Land Cover, which classify land more precisely than an NDVI threshold and can rule out protected areas, agricultural land, or urban zones directly.
Grid capacity and substation data, which national grid operators sometimes publish, going beyond simple proximity to a power line to also account for whether that line actually has spare capacity.
Multi-criteria decision analysis methods, such as the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), which are commonly used in the literature to justify the weights assigned to each suitability factor, rather than choosing them by hand as this course does.







TipWhere to look for more



A good starting point is searching for terms such as “solar site suitability GIS AHP” or “renewable energy site selection multi-criteria” in Google Scholar, which surfaces a large number of peer-reviewed studies describing exactly which datasets and weighting schemes they used for similar projects in different countries.
